Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion When the outrage dies, who remembers the victims? – The Obuasi SHTS case and our troubling habit of forgetting the people behind the headlines Source : She Captures Humanity 12 November 2026 2:45pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The speed at which victims of sexual abuse, especially children, can become less central to the public discussion of their experience once the outrage dies away is deeply troubling.
A common pattern exists in the manner in which we typically respond to unsettling stories in our region. A tragedy occurs, an inquiry reveals some unpleasant truth, social media erupts with outrage, high-profile individuals offer their condolences and opinions, and citizens call for accountability.
Depending on the degree of disturbance created by the story, national discussion can dominate public discourse anywhere from a couple of days to several weeks. Once another story begins to gather attention, public focus will shift, and the individuals at the center of the original scandal will be left to deal with the consequences of the scandal, usually without the same amount of public outcry that originally surrounded them.
The recent allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) have once again brought questions of child protection, institutional accountability and the safety of girls into Ghana's national conversation. Following an investigation by Joy News, the case prompted public outrage, government intervention and renewed scrutiny of the Ghana Education Service and its handling of complaints.
The headmaster has been interdicted pending investigations, while the education ministry has announced support for 19 students identified in connection with the allegations, including psychological counselling, medical care and academic assistance.
Each of these actions is an essential measure. However, I am currently focused on a larger question. What happens when the public stops paying attention?
Because the uncomfortable reality is that the consequences of abuse do not disappear when a story stops trending. The fear, trauma, disruption to education, and struggle to rebuild a sense of safety do not operate on the same timeline as public outrage.
One of the most troubling aspects of our response to humanitarian and social issues is how easily we become invested in the story but lose sight of the people experiencing it.
We remember the headline and the outrage and debate who should be held responsible. Yet how often do we return to ask whether the people affected are actually receiving the support they were promised?
In cases involving sexual abuse, particularly where children are concerned, the need for sustained attention is even greater. The immediate public reaction may create pressure for intervention, but recovery and protection require much more than a moment of national sympathy.
For the students at Obuasi, the questions above should not conclude with an announcement stating that counseling and medical support will be provided. Will these services be provided? Will their academic development be supported? Will they be free from intimidation, victim-blaming, and unwanted public attention, and will their identities remain protected?
Each of these points represents a critical component of what a meaningful response should look like.
We must be careful not to assume that an announcement means an intervention has been fully implemented. Equally, we should not assume that nothing is being done simply because the public has not received every detail. What we need is appropriate transparency, sustained monitoring and evidence that the commitments made are translating into actual support.
This problem extends beyond Obuasi and beyond sexual abuse cases.
Disturbing cases of violence against women, child exploitation, among others occasionally generate sufficient national interest to warrant national attention. We show outrage over such cases and declare our solidarity with victims. Yet we frequently lack the ability to sustain our outrage beyond the initial controversy.
Consider the reported sexual abuse of a 14-year-old autistic student at Bolgatanga Girls' Senior High School, which also reignited conversations about safeguarding and the vulnerability of children within educational institutions in September 2026.
Different cases have different circumstances, and should be investigated on their own evidence. However, recurring concerns about the protection of students should prompt us to examine whether our responses are producing lasting improvements or simply reacting to each new incident.
We cannot keep treating every disturbing revelation as an isolated controversy when similar questions about reporting, institutional responsibility and student safety continue to arise.
The problem with reactive advocacy is that it places enormous attention on the moment of exposure but often insufficient attention on what follows. We become passionate about demanding action when a story is fresh, but less consistent in monitoring whether that action has happened.
And when public attention disappears, the pressure on institutions to demonstrate progress can disappear with it.
One of the most significant lessons learned from the Obuasi case is that children should never suffer as a result of whether or not an investigative journalist exposes a problem or whether enough public outrage exists to compel action from authorities.
Schools and educational authorities have responsibilities that exist regardless of whether or not the public is watching.
As a young woman involved in humanitarian work and women's rights advocacy, I believe one of the largest challenges facing social advocacy is not always getting people to care. Sometimes it is getting them to continue caring long after the initial emotional response has passed.
There is a difference between feeling sorry for someone and committing to support them, a difference between demanding justice and ensuring that justice was pursued, and there is a difference between sharing a story and being responsible for ensuring that the issues raised by that story were not forgotten.
This is why journalists, civil society organisations, child protection advocates, women's rights groups and concerned citizens must continue asking questions long after the initial headlines disappear.
We must follow up on investigations, monitor institutional commitments, demand appropriate updates and keep the needs of affected people in public conversation without compromising their privacy or dignity.
Our advocacy must also extend beyond individual controversies to the policies, safeguards and social attitudes that allow harm to occur in the first place.
The students of Obuasi and every victim of sexual abuse deserve more than just a moment of national sympathy. They deserve protection, support, a credible process for establishing the facts and an educational environment in which their safety is taken seriously. The headmaster is equally entitled to due process, and allegations must be established through the appropriate legal processes. Neither principle should be sacrificed.
Ultimately, the measure of our concern cannot be how loudly we react when a disturbing story breaks. It must also be how consistently we demand answers when the excitement has passed.
The people behind our headlines do not get to move on simply because the rest of us have. If our outrage disappears before their painful experience had been addressed and prior to any accountability having been secured, then perhaps we must begin to question whether or not our outrage was worth anything.
